The Spotted sucker (Minytrema melanops) attains a maximum recorded total length of 50 centimeters [Li = 50 centimeters] in the wild, a size that places it among the larger members of the Catostomidae family. Growth data from long-term mark-recapture studies in southeastern United States river systems indicate that females reach reproductive maturity at a total length of 29 centimeters [Lp = 29 centimeters], a metric that corresponds well with the estimated age at puberty of three to four years derived from scale annuli analysis. Newly hatched larvae emerge from demersal eggs that are relatively small, with each freshly spawned ovum yielding a yolk-sac larva whose initial wet weight at birth is approximately 0.0058 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0058 grams]. This modest starting mass reflects the limited endogenous yolk reserves available to the endotrophic larva during its brief lecithotrophic phase before the onset of exogenous feeding. The species exhibits a growth trajectory that is typical of many riverine catostomids, with juvenile fish accumulating tissue steadily across the first several growing seasons.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the maximum reproductive rate of the Spotted sucker has been quantified through detailed gravimetric analyses of ovarian tissue. Gravid females in their peak reproductive condition produce an average of 25.5 eggs per gram of body weight, and given a single spawning event per year [F_R_i = single spawning event per year], a typical adult carrying roughly 1,280 grams [Wwi = roughly 1,280 grams] of somatic mass deposits approximately 32,640 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 32,640 eggs per spawning event]. This batch-fecundity pattern aligns with the reproductive strategy documented in other iteroparous catostomids inhabiting warm-water systems. The temperature dependence of oocyte development is notable; at cooler thermal regimes, vitellogenesis proceeds more slowly and the resultant clutch sizes are often reduced, highlighting the importance of thermal conditions in regulating gametogenic output.

The ultimate wet weight achieved by adult Spotted sucker individuals is approximately 1,280 grams [Wwi = approximately 1,280 grams], a figure derived from length-weight regressions applied to the maximum body length of 50 centimeters. This asymptotic mass is attained gradually over the species' lifespan, with the most rapid gains occurring during the juvenile and sub-adult stages before the energetic demands of gonadal development begin to divert resources away from body growth. Field surveys consistently show that the heaviest specimens are those exceeding 40 centimeters in total length, and these large adults frequently dominate the spawning aggregations that form in shallow gravel runs during the spring. The relationship between length and mass is strongly allometric, following a cubic function typical of fishes, such that a small increase in linear dimensions yields a disproportionately large increase in body mass. This mass gain is critical for females, as body size is positively correlated with fecundity across a wide range of catostomid taxa, reinforcing the selective advantage of sustained growth beyond the onset of maturity.

Longevity records for the Spotted sucker, based on otolith-derived age estimates from fish captured in multiple drainages across the species' native range, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 8 years [am = approximately 8 years] under natural thermal conditions averaging 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This lifespan is intermediate among the Catostomidae, whose members span from short-lived species persisting only three to four years to long-lived forms exceeding two decades. Mortality schedules appear to be age-dependent, with the highest attrition occurring during the yolk-sac larval and early juvenile stages, where predation and starvation pressure are intense. Once individuals surpass the first winter, annual survival rates increase markedly, and a substantial proportion of three- and four-year-old fish survive to reproduce in multiple consecutive spawning runs. The relatively extended post-maturity lifespan supports an iteroparous breeding strategy, allowing females to spread reproductive effort across several years and thereby buffer against the stochastic environmental variability characteristic of warm-water streams. Senescence-related mortality becomes apparent after the seventh year, with declining condition factors and reduced fecundity observed in the oldest age classes.

Comparative analyses of reproductive allocation among riverine catostomids reveal that the Spotted sucker's investment per offspring is modest, given that the wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0058 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0058 grams] is among the lower values recorded for the genus Minytrema. This small birth mass is offset by a high fecundity, as the estimated 32,640 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 32,640 eggs per spawning event] produced during a single spawning at 18 °C [T = 18 °C] ensures that even moderate-sized females contribute thousands of ova to the larval pool each spring. The species' asymptotic length of 50 centimeters [Li = 50 centimeters] and ultimate wet weight of 1,280 grams [Wwi = 1,280 grams] together define the upper boundary of its life-history space, within which growth, reproduction, and survival trade-offs are negotiated. Females first spawn after reaching a total length of 29 centimeters [Lp = 29 centimeters] and continue to grow slowly thereafter, channelling surplus energy into both daily metabolic costs and gamete production across a lifespan of 8 years [am = 8 years] at 18 °C at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This integrated life-history pattern underscores the species' adaptation to productive riverine habitats where early maturity and high fecundity compensate for elevated juvenile mortality.
